facts.fact: The Americans with Disabilities Act was enacted in 1990 and is the civil-rights law that frames website accessibility obligations in the U.S.
facts.quote: The **Americans with Disabilities Act**, enacted in **1990**, is the civil-rights law that frames website accessibility obligations in the U.S.

facts.fact: The Department of Justice has tied web compliance for government entities to WCAG 2.1 Level AA, as stated in the DOJ's small-entity compliance guide.
facts.quote: the Department of Justice has tied web compliance to WCAG 2.1 Level AA, with compliance dates set for April 26, 2027

facts.fact: DOJ web compliance dates for public entities are April 26, 2027 for entities serving 50,000 people or more, and April 26, 2028 for smaller public entities and special districts.
facts.quote: compliance dates set for April 26, 2027 for entities serving 50,000 people or more and April 26, 2028 for smaller public entities and special districts

facts.fact: The ADA statute does not give private businesses the same specific web accessibility rule that DOJ sets for government entities.
facts.quote: The ADA statute does not give private businesses the same specific rule.

facts.fact: The article recommends WCAG 2.2 Level AA as the planning target for private-sector small business sites.
facts.quote: In most cases, **WCAG 2.2 Level AA** is the right planning target for private-sector sites

facts.fact: WCAG is organized around four principles.
facts.quote: WCAG is built around four principles.

facts.fact: The article's DIY website accessibility review has three parts: automated code-level scanning, testing key tasks without a mouse, and checking whether the page makes sense without visual styling.
facts.quote: a useful DIY review has three parts: scan for code-level issues, test key tasks without a mouse, and check whether the page still makes sense without its visual styling.

facts.fact: Small-business guidance cited by Adwave, based on the NFIB resource, sets a practical contrast benchmark of at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text.
facts.quote: at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text

facts.fact: Adwave states that no content should flash more than three times per second as part of its flash and seizure risk check.
facts.quote: No content should flash more than three times per second.

facts.fact: Per the cited overview, the DOJ finalized a rule for state and local government websites in April 2024.
facts.quote: especially after the DOJ finalized its April 2024 rule for state and local government websites

facts.fact: The vendor recommends re-testing primary user paths with keyboard testing every quarter.
facts.quote: Re-test primary user paths such as contact, booking, checkout, quote request, and navigation.

facts.fact: The vendor recommends a monthly review of newly published pages, blog posts, forms, and media for alt text, headings, captions, and readable links.
facts.quote: Check newly published pages, blog posts, forms, and media for alt text, headings, captions, and readable links.

facts.fact: The vendor states that a website accessibility statement should name the standard being targeted, which is typically WCAG Level AA.
facts.quote: State the benchmark you're working toward, typically WCAG Level AA.

facts.fact: The vendor describes WCAG 2.2 Level AA as a sensible target for most small business websites today.
facts.quote: WCAG 2.2 Level AA is a sensible target for most small business websites today.

facts.fact: The vendor says WCAG 2.1 AA is still a workable starting point for sites whose developer or platform still references it, especially when budget is tight.
facts.quote: If your developer or platform still references WCAG 2.1 AA, that is still a workable starting point, especially if budget is tight.

facts.fact: The vendor states that an accessibility statement does not by itself make an inaccessible website compliant.
facts.quote: An accessibility statement won't make an inaccessible website compliant.
